about: Story bible of the running startup, in machine-readable form, for the continuity check. The human version is _build/style/STARTUP.md. If the two differ, this file wins. Every number here is the startup's own invented number. No AWS limit, price or behaviour is stated here: AWS facts come only from the fact canon.
file_name_note: The file is data/startup.json (it was harken.json until 2026-10-09). Harken was the working name of the startup. The name is now Callvale.

company.name: Callvale
company.name_meaning: Vale is an old word for valley: the place where the calls collect.
five_lines: Callvale sells a call-intelligence service. Customers send recorded or live support calls and get transcripts, sentiment, topics, summaries, search and dashboards.
The customers are customer-support teams: first of small software companies, later of a bank and a hospital group.
The customers care about compliance because recordings contain personal data, card numbers and health information, and regulators ask the customers for proof.
The customers care about private connectivity because a bank does not send customer calls through the public internet.
The customers care about recovery because support teams work from the recordings every day, and the bank's contract sets an RPO of 15 minutes and an RTO of 1 hour.

stages.name: Demo day
stages.trigger: A demo for investors works. Three pilot teams start to upload real calls.
stages.end_state: One hand-built instance in the default VPC runs the web application, the processing jobs and the database. The root user's access key is in the code. The audio bucket is public. This is the before picture.

stages.name: First ten customers
stages.trigger: Ten paying customers arrive with purchase forms about security. In the same month, the only volume fills up.
stages.end_state: IAM roles for workloads and IAM users with MFA for people. A private bucket with presigned URLs and a lifecycle rule. A custom VPC in two Availability Zones with one NAT gateway and an S3 gateway endpoint. One web instance and one worker instance from an AMI. Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with a Multi-AZ deployment.

stages.name: Launch week
stages.trigger: A load test at month 11 fails. The public launch at month 12 brings 8 times the normal traffic: the web tier holds, but the pipeline fails on launch day. The AWS credits end at month 17.
stages.end_state: CloudFront and Route 53 in front of an Application Load Balancer and a web Auto Scaling group in three Availability Zones. Uploads flow through queues, functions and one state machine. Job state is in DynamoDB. Shared files are on Amazon EFS, sessions in Amazon ElastiCache. A public API with Amazon API Gateway and Amazon Cognito.

stages.name: First bank customer
stages.trigger: Ostell Bank signs for 3 years and sends a security questionnaire of 180 questions. Chen joins. Dorrin Health signs at month 21.
stages.end_state: Seven accounts with IAM Identity Center. Customer managed keys, rotated secrets, AWS WAF, the detection services, monitoring and an audit trail. AWS PrivateLink, Site-to-Site VPN and Direct Connect to the bank. Six services on AWS Fargate, Amazon Aurora, AWS Backup, and three intake paths for bulk data.

stages.name: Global and efficient
stages.trigger: The bank contract needs a second Region by month 27. Callvale Live starts. Callvale acquires Peldon Systems. Ana orders a cost review.
stages.end_state: Everything from templates. Warm standby in US West (Oregon). A live event stream and a data lake. Peldon's servers and databases in AWS. AWS Batch for the bulk job, five new AI features, a Savings Plan and Spot Instances.

story_order_rule: A component exists only from the chapter that adds it, in this order. The before picture of a chapter is the state after all earlier chapters in this order.

P1.state: The web application calls the one worker directly and waits. Scheduled jobs on the worker register uploads, save results and send notifications. Job status is in PostgreSQL.

P2.state: S3 event, uploads queue, start-job function, convert queue, conversion workers in an Auto Scaling group that scales from 0 to 40 on the backlog. A chain of functions calls Amazon Transcribe and Amazon Comprehend and waits in loops. The save-results function stores the results. The topic transcript-ready fans out to the queues webhooks and indexing. Job status is still in PostgreSQL, through Amazon RDS Proxy.

P3.state: The start-job function starts the state machine call-pipeline. Its six states are convert (through the convert queue), transcribe, analyze, summarize, save and notify. Job state is in the DynamoDB table jobs.

pipeline_states.rule: Chapters 31 and 18 share one before picture (P1) and one after picture (P2). Chapters 32 and 28 share P2 and P3. Each chapter highlights its own part.

02.title: The AWS map: global infrastructure, shared responsibility, Well-Architected
02.trigger: Demo day goes well. An investor asks for a technical review, so you run a first Well-Architected review with Ana and Ben.
02.problem: Callvale runs its whole product on one instance in one Availability Zone. Ben created everything by hand with the root user. Three pilot teams upload real customer calls. The founders must choose a Region and must learn which protections are their own responsibility.
02.adds_note: Nothing is built. The review lists 12 high-risk findings: the flawed start.

US East (N. Virginia), near the first customers
two Regions from the first day
decision.choice: US East (N. Virginia), planned for three Availability Zones.
decision.tradeoff: A Region failure stops the service. Callvale accepts this risk until stage 4.

question.text: AWS says that it is secure. So why is the public bucket our problem and not theirs?

03.title: IAM
03.trigger: A customer's purchase form asks who can access the recordings. Ben finds the root user's access key in the code and on three laptops.
03.problem: Callvale's application calls Amazon S3 and Amazon Transcribe with the root user's access key. The key is stored in the code. Ana and Ben share the root user's password. Callvale must remove long-term keys and must give each person and each workload least privilege.
adds: IAM role with an instance profile
IAM users with MFA in two groups

options: move the access key out of the code
an IAM user with an access key for each workload
an IAM role on the instance
decision.choice: An IAM role for the workload. People sign in with IAM users and MFA for now.
decision.tradeoff: Each workload needs its own tested policy. IAM users stay until IAM Identity Center replaces them at stage 3.

question.text: If I delete the access key, how does the code on the instance get permission to read the bucket?

03.diagram: Before: one root access key in the code and on three laptops. After: the application assumes a role; people are IAM users with MFA; the root user is locked away.

later.note: Cross-account roles for the seven accounts (chapter 04). IAM Identity Center replaces the IAM users (chapter 05).

03.note: The story shows what four people did in one account. The chapter body still gives the current AWS recommendation for human access, from the canon.

04.title: Organizations, SCPs, Control Tower and RAM
04.trigger: Ostell Bank's questionnaire asks how production is separated from testing. Everything is in one account. Chen joins Callvale to lead security.
04.problem: Callvale runs development, testing and production in one AWS account. The bank requires an isolated production environment and audit logs that operators cannot change. No workload can run outside two approved Regions. The rules must apply to every account, including future accounts.

options: one account, separated by tags and IAM policies
several accounts, each configured by hand
AWS Control Tower with service control policies
decision.choice: AWS Control Tower with seven accounts in three organizational units, and service control policies.
decision.tradeoff: Seven accounts need more design for access between them. Some rules block engineers until an exception is designed.

question.text: How do I make sure that even a production administrator cannot turn off the audit log?

04.diagram: Before: one account holds development, testing and production. After: the organization tree with seven accounts in three organizational units, and service control policies on the units.
04.note: AWS RAM shares the transit gateway of chapter 11 with the workload accounts.

05.title: IAM Identity Center, Directory Service and Cognito
05.trigger: Seven accounts would mean seven IAM users for each engineer. The bank also wants its 400 supervisors to sign in with the bank's identity provider.
05.problem: Callvale's 14 engineers need one sign-in for seven AWS accounts, with no long-term credentials. Separately, 400 bank employees must sign in to the Callvale web application with their corporate identities. Callvale must not store their passwords.
adds: Amazon Cognito federation with the bank's SAML identity provider

options: IAM users in every account
IAM users in one account who assume roles in the others
IAM Identity Center connected to Callvale's identity provider
decision.choice: IAM Identity Center with permission sets for engineers. Amazon Cognito federation for the bank's supervisors.
decision.tradeoff: All AWS access depends on the identity provider. Callvale must keep one tested emergency access path.

06.title: KMS and CloudHSM
06.trigger: The questionnaire asks who controls the keys for the bank's recordings, and how Callvale proves each use of a key.
06.problem: Callvale encrypts its buckets and its database with keys that AWS manages. The bank requires that Callvale controls who can use the key for the bank's recordings. Every use of the key must be logged. Access must end quickly when the contract ends.

options: keep the keys that AWS manages
customer managed keys in AWS KMS
keys in AWS CloudHSM
decision.choice: Customer managed keys in AWS KMS, with one dedicated key for the bank's recordings.
decision.tradeoff: A wrong key policy can stop the pipeline. Key requests add a cost that grows with volume.

question.text: If an engineer has full S3 permissions, can that engineer still read the bank's recordings?

later.note: For the second Region (chapter 40).

07.title: Secrets Manager, Parameter Store and ACM
07.trigger: The questionnaire asks how often database passwords change. The honest answer is never: one password has been in a configuration file from stage 1.
07.problem: Callvale stores the database password in a configuration file on each instance. The password has never changed. The bank requires rotation every 30 days with no downtime and no new deployment. Callvale also wants TLS certificates that renew without manual work.

options: an encrypted file in Amazon S3
Parameter Store for everything
Secrets Manager for database credentials, Parameter Store for plain configuration
decision.choice: Secrets Manager with automatic rotation for database credentials. Parameter Store for plain configuration.
decision.tradeoff: Secrets Manager adds a cost for each secret. The application must read the secret at run time and reconnect after a rotation.

question.text: Parameter Store or Secrets Manager? I want one place for configuration. Which one, and why?

07.diagram: Before: one password in a file on every instance. After: the application's role reads a rotated secret; ACM certificates sit on the load balancer and on CloudFront.
07.note: ACM certificates are in use from stage 2 (chapters 14 and 15).

08.title: WAF, Shield, Firewall Manager and Network Firewall
08.trigger: In one hour, 60,000 automated sign-in attempts arrive from 1,400 IP addresses. The questionnaire also asks about outbound traffic control.
08.problem: Callvale's sign-in page receives 60,000 automated attempts in one hour from 1,400 IP addresses. The bank also requires that production workloads connect only to approved outside domains. Callvale must block common web attacks and limit request rates in every account.

options: block the attacking IP addresses in network ACLs
AWS WAF with managed rules and a rate-based rule
AWS WAF plus AWS Shield Advanced
decision.choice: AWS WAF on CloudFront and on the load balancer, applied to all accounts by AWS Firewall Manager.
decision.tradeoff: Callvale has no paid DDoS support during a very large attack. Rate limits need tuning for users who share one address.

question.text: The attack came from 1,400 addresses. Why can we not block those addresses?

08.diagram: Before: the sign-in flood reaches the application. After: a WAF web ACL on CloudFront stops it; outbound traffic passes through AWS Network Firewall to approved domains.
08.note: AWS Shield Advanced is weighed and not bought.

09.title: GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, Security Hub, Detective, Config and Artifact
09.trigger: Most of the 43 'no' answers on the questionnaire ask one thing: can Callvale detect a problem and show evidence?
09.problem: Callvale cannot answer the bank's questions about changes in production, card numbers in transcripts, software vulnerabilities and stolen credentials. Callvale needs continuous detection in all seven accounts. The findings must appear in one place.

options: a weekly manual checklist
open-source scanners that Callvale runs on EC2
managed detection services for the whole organization
decision.choice: The managed services, turned on for all accounts, with findings in AWS Security Hub in the security account.
decision.tradeoff: Every finding needs an owner. Each service adds a cost that grows with data and events.

question.text: Seven services with similar names. Which one answers which of the bank's questions?

09.diagram: A map from question to service: threats, vulnerabilities, sensitive data, configuration changes, AWS audit reports. All findings flow into AWS Security Hub.
09.note: Story event: the first Amazon Macie job finds card numbers in 1,300 transcripts. From then on, the analyze step removes card numbers before the pipeline stores a transcript. AWS Artifact gives Chen the audit reports of AWS for the bank.

10.title: Amazon VPC
10.trigger: The purchase form asks if the database is reachable from the internet. It is: all three instances have public IP addresses.
10.problem: Callvale's web, worker and database instances run in the default VPC with public IP addresses. The database must not be reachable from the internet. The worker must still download software updates. Its large transfers to Amazon S3 must not pass through a NAT device.
adds: custom VPC with public and private subnets in two Availability Zones

options: stay in the default VPC and tighten the security groups
a custom VPC with one NAT gateway and an S3 gateway endpoint
a custom VPC with a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone
decision.choice: A custom VPC with one NAT gateway and a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3.
decision.tradeoff: If the Availability Zone of the NAT gateway fails, private subnets lose outbound internet access. Callvale accepts this until stage 2.

question.text: My worker only talks to S3. Why do I pay for a NAT gateway at all?

10.diagram: Before: three instances with public IP addresses in the default VPC. After: web instance in a public subnet; worker and database in private subnets; one NAT gateway; an S3 gateway endpoint.

later.note: A third Availability Zone, and a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone.
Interface endpoints and a transit gateway (chapter 11).

11.title: Connecting VPCs: peering, Transit Gateway, endpoints and PrivateLink
11.trigger: The bank's own application runs in the bank's VPC. The bank forbids vendor traffic on the internet, and both VPCs use 10.20.0.0/16.
11.problem: The bank's application, in the bank's VPC, must call Callvale's API without using the internet. Both VPCs use the CIDR block 10.20.0.0/16. The bank must not reach anything else in Callvale's VPC. Callvale's workloads must also call AWS services privately.

options: a VPC peering connection with the bank
a transit gateway shared with the bank
an AWS PrivateLink endpoint service
decision.choice: An endpoint service. The bank creates an interface endpoint in its own VPC.
decision.tradeoff: The bank reaches one service in one direction. Each further service needs its own endpoint service and adds fixed cost.

question.text: With a peering connection, the two networks would be joined. How does PrivateLink limit the bank to the API?

11.diagram: Before: bank application, internet, public API. After: interface endpoint in the bank's VPC, endpoint service, Network Load Balancer, Callvale's API. Callvale's VPCs connect through a transit gateway.
11.note: The transit gateway is in the network account and connects Callvale's own VPCs, the VPN and Direct Connect. A VPC peering connection is weighed and not used.

12.title: Site-to-Site VPN, Direct Connect and Client VPN
12.trigger: The bank's call recorder runs in a data center in New Jersey. Recordings must reach Callvale every night, and the bank starts in 3 weeks.
12.problem: The bank's data center must send recordings to Callvale's VPC every night. An encrypted connection must be ready in 3 weeks. Within 6 months, the bank requires a private connection with consistent throughput. Callvale's engineers also need access to a private admin tool.

options: AWS Site-to-Site VPN only
wait for AWS Direct Connect
VPN now, Direct Connect later, VPN kept for backup
decision.choice: VPN in 5 days, in time for the bank's start. Direct Connect arrives after 10 weeks and becomes the main path. The VPN stays for backup.
decision.tradeoff: Two connections to configure and monitor. Direct Connect adds a fixed monthly cost and a long delivery time.

question.text: The bank says that Direct Connect is private. Does private mean encrypted?

12.diagram: Before: the bank's data center uploads through the internet. After: Direct Connect is the main path and Site-to-Site VPN the backup, both to the transit gateway; engineers use Client VPN.

later.note: To Peldon's data center, for the migration (chapter 39).

13.title: Amazon Route 53
13.trigger: Before launch, callvale.example still points to the IP address of one old instance at the registrar.
13.problem: Callvale's domain is hosted at a registrar. The name callvale.example points to the IP address of one old instance. Before launch, callvale.example and app.callvale.example must point to AWS resources by name. Later, DNS must send users to a second Region after a failure.

options: keep DNS at the registrar and use CNAME records
an Elastic IP address on one instance
a Route 53 hosted zone with alias records
decision.choice: A Route 53 public hosted zone with alias records for CloudFront and for the load balancer.
decision.tradeoff: DNS answers are cached by resolvers, so every change needs planning. Route 53 is one more service to learn.

question.text: Why can I not point an A record at the IP address of the load balancer?

13.diagram: Before: registrar DNS; callvale.example points to one IP address. After: Route 53 alias records point both names to CloudFront. Stage 4 adds a failover record pair with a health check.

later.note: Failover records for the load balancers in the two Regions (chapter 40).

14.title: Elastic Load Balancing
14.trigger: The launch date is fixed. In a load test, the single web instance fails at 150 requests per second.
14.problem: Callvale's web application runs on one instance in one Availability Zone. A load test fails at 150 requests per second. The application must survive the loss of an instance or an Availability Zone. It must serve HTTPS and must route requests by URL path later.
adds: Application Load Balancer in three Availability Zones
HTTPS listener with an ACM certificate

options: a spare instance and an Elastic IP address that Ben moves by hand
a Network Load Balancer
an Application Load Balancer
decision.choice: An Application Load Balancer in three Availability Zones, with one web instance in each.
decision.tradeoff: The load balancer costs money at night too. Sessions in instance memory now need sticky sessions until chapter 29.

question.text: Application Load Balancer or Network Load Balancer: what decides it for a web application like ours?

14.diagram: Before: users, one instance. After: users, Application Load Balancer in three public subnets, instances in three private subnets, one instance marked unhealthy.

later.note: In front of the PrivateLink endpoint service (chapter 11).
For live audio, behind AWS Global Accelerator (chapter 15).

15.title: CloudFront and Global Accelerator
15.trigger: Before launch, 70% of web requests are for static files, and 20% of users are outside the United States.
15.problem: Instances in one Region serve every request, and 70% of requests are for static files. Recordings are in a private bucket. Only signed-in users can play a recording, for a limited time. Callvale must reduce instance load and latency without making the bucket public.
adds: origin access control for the S3 origins

options: a larger web tier and presigned URLs from the Region
CloudFront for static files only
CloudFront in front of everything, with private S3 origins and signed URLs
decision.choice: CloudFront in front of the web application, the static files and the recordings.
decision.tradeoff: Cached files can be old after a release, so each release needs versioned file names or an invalidation.

question.text: Does the bucket have to be public for CloudFront to serve our recordings?

15.diagram: Before: all users reach instances in one Region. After: users reach the nearest edge location; static files come from the cache; recordings need a signed URL; only API calls reach the load balancer.

later.note: Fixed IP addresses for live.callvale.example, in front of the live-audio Network Load Balancers in both Regions. The bank's firewall team allows fixed addresses only.

16.title: Amazon EC2
16.trigger: The demo-day instance is large and almost idle. Nobody remembers how it was installed, and port 22 is open to the world.
16.problem: Callvale's single instance was installed by hand. Average CPU use is 9%, with peaks of 85% on weekday mornings. Administrators connect with SSH from any IP address. Callvale must launch identical instances in minutes, pay less for idle capacity, and close the administration port.

options: keep the large instance and restrict SSH to the office IP address
resize the instance in place
rebuild from an AMI, split the roles, connect with Session Manager
decision.choice: Rebuild from an AMI and a launch template. Split web, worker and database. Use Session Manager, with port 22 closed.
decision.tradeoff: Every change must go into the image or the start configuration, so quick fixes on a running instance stop.

question.text: The instance is at 9% most of the day. Are we paying for a size that we do not need?

16.diagram: Before: one large hand-built instance with port 22 open. After: AMI, launch template, three smaller instances; Session Manager with no inbound port.

later.note: Auto Scaling groups use the launch template (chapter 17).
Spot Instances for conversion workers and a Savings Plan for steady compute (chapter 41).

16.note: The story names instance families by purpose only: a burstable instance for web, a compute optimized instance for the worker. An exact instance type appears only with a fact link.

17.title: EC2 Auto Scaling
17.trigger: The same load test. Traffic also has a fixed shape: the peak comes from 09:00 to 11:00 Eastern on weekdays.
17.problem: Callvale's web tier needs 3 instances at night and up to 12 at peak. The peak comes every weekday from 09:00 to 11:00. A new instance needs 4 minutes before it serves traffic. Callvale must replace failed instances automatically and must not pay for 12 instances all day.
adds: EC2 Auto Scaling group for the web tier

options: 12 instances all the time
scheduled scaling only
target tracking plus a scheduled action at 08:45 on weekdays
decision.choice: Target tracking, with a scheduled action that raises capacity to 6 at 08:45 on weekdays. Minimum 3, maximum 12.
decision.tradeoff: A sudden spike is still served late by about 4 minutes, so the minimum stays at 3.

question.text: The load balancer has health checks. Is it not the load balancer that replaces a broken instance?

17.diagram: Before: one fixed instance under a traffic curve with a morning peak. After: capacity follows the curve: a scheduled step at 08:45, target tracking above it, minimum 3.

adds: EC2 Auto Scaling group for conversion workers
later.note: After launch day, 0 to 40 conversion workers scale on the backlog of the convert queue (chapter 31).
The web group is retired when the services move to AWS Fargate (chapter 19). The worker group stays.

18.title: AWS Lambda
18.trigger: On launch day the one worker cannot keep up. The small scheduled jobs on the same instance stop with it.
18.problem: Small jobs run on a schedule on Callvale's worker instance: register an upload, save results, send a notification. Each job runs for seconds, thousands of times in the morning and rarely at night. When the worker is busy, the jobs stop. Callvale wants them to run for each event at no idle cost.

options: the same jobs on a larger worker instance
containers that run all day
AWS Lambda functions that events invoke
decision.choice: Lambda functions. The start-job function polls the uploads queue.
decision.tradeoff: Long audio conversions do not fit and stay on the workers. Functions that use the database need Amazon RDS Proxy.

question.text: Why not move the audio conversion to Lambda too, and delete the workers?

18.diagram: Before: scheduled jobs inside the worker instance. After: S3 event, uploads queue, start-job function, convert queue, conversion workers; the functions save-results and notify finish the job.
18.note: Pipeline state P1 before, P2 after, shared with chapter 31.

19.title: ECS, EKS, Fargate and ECR
19.trigger: 14 engineers release one application together. One release takes 40 minutes, and one bad change in billing breaks sign-in.
19.problem: Callvale's application runs on an Auto Scaling group of instances that the team must patch. 14 engineers release it together, and one release takes 40 minutes. Callvale wants six services that deploy and scale separately, with no instances to patch. One engineer knows Kubernetes.

options: six Auto Scaling groups of instances
Amazon EKS
Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate
decision.choice: Six Amazon ECS services on AWS Fargate: dashboard, upload, search, accounts, billing, admin.
decision.tradeoff: Callvale has less control of the host and pays more for each unit of compute than on well-used instances.

question.text: ECS or EKS? My one Kubernetes engineer says that EKS is the standard.

19.diagram: Before: one application on the web Auto Scaling group. After: the load balancer routes by path to six Fargate services; images come from Amazon ECR; conversion workers stay on EC2.
19.note: The Network Load Balancer of the PrivateLink endpoint service now forwards to the upload service. Amazon Inspector scans the images in Amazon ECR.

20.title: More compute: Beanstalk, Batch, Outposts, Local Zones, Wavelength
20.trigger: The bank buys analysis of its imported archive: 6.7 million recordings, to finish in 30 days.
20.problem: Callvale must process 6.7 million archived recordings within 30 days. Each recording is processed alone in about 90 seconds and can start again after an interruption. The job runs one time. Callvale wants the lowest compute cost and does not want to build a job scheduler.

options: a higher maximum for the worker Auto Scaling group
one AWS Lambda invocation for each recording
AWS Batch on Spot Instances
decision.choice: AWS Batch with a managed compute environment on Spot Instances.
decision.tradeoff: An interrupted job starts again, so some work is done twice. The team learns one more service for a single job.

question.text: It is a single job. What is the cheapest way to finish it in 30 days?

20.diagram: A map of Callvale's four kinds of compute: Fargate services, EC2 Spot workers, Lambda functions, the AWS Batch job. The services that Callvale does not use are greyed.
20.note: Not used: AWS Elastic Beanstalk, AWS Local Zones, AWS Wavelength, AWS Serverless Application Repository. AWS Outposts: the bank asked at stage 3 if Callvale could process calls inside the bank's data center, and Callvale declined. VMware Cloud on AWS: weighed for Peldon in chapter 39.

21.title: Amazon S3
21.trigger: A pilot customer discovers that anyone who has the link can download a recording. The audio bucket has been public from demo day.
21.problem: Callvale stores recordings in a public bucket so that the browser can play them. Recordings contain personal data and must be private. Customers must still upload and play recordings from the browser. Callvale keeps recordings for 7 years, and 2% are opened after 90 days.
adds: S3 Lifecycle rule to S3 Standard-IA

options: a public bucket with long random object names
a private bucket, with all transfers through the application instance
a private bucket with presigned URLs
decision.choice: A private bucket with presigned URLs: 15 minutes for an upload, 5 minutes for playback.
decision.tradeoff: A presigned URL works for anyone who holds it until it expires. The application must create one for each transfer.

question.text: How can a customer upload directly to our bucket if the bucket is private?

21.diagram: Before: browser, public bucket, anyone with the link. After: the browser gets a presigned URL and uploads to the private bucket; a lifecycle rule moves recordings to S3 Standard-IA after 90 days.

later.note: For the bank's prefix ostell/ (chapters 06 and 42).
Replication to the second Region (chapter 40). The archive storage class for old recordings (chapter 41).

21.note: The lifecycle rule applies to the audio bucket only. Transcripts are small (30 KB on average) and stay in S3 Standard: a good Spot the bug.

22.title: EBS and instance store
22.trigger: On a Tuesday at 09:40, the only volume fills up. The database stops for 3 hours, and the newest backup is 9 days old.
22.problem: One volume holds the operating system, the database and temporary audio files. The volume filled up and the database stopped for 3 hours. The newest backup was 9 days old. Callvale must lose at most 24 hours of data and must recover within 8 hours.
adds: daily snapshots with Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager

options: a larger single volume
a separate data volume with daily snapshots
move the database to a managed service now
decision.choice: A separate gp3 data volume for the database, with daily snapshots kept for 30 days.
decision.tradeoff: The database still depends on one instance in one Availability Zone. Chapter 26 removes that risk two months later.

question.text: If that instance fails tomorrow, what do we lose, and how long are we offline?

22.diagram: Before: one full volume holds everything. After: a root volume and a separate data volume; a timeline of daily snapshots.

later.note: Conversion workers keep the temporary files of one call on instance store volumes.

23.title: EFS and FSx
23.trigger: With several web instances, a report created on one instance cannot be downloaded from another. Conversion workers also need a shared work directory.
23.problem: Callvale's application writes report files to the volume of the instance that creates them. A download request often reaches another instance. Linux conversion workers also need one shared directory for large temporary files. The application code that reads and writes files cannot change this year.
adds: mount targets in three Availability Zones

options: sticky sessions, so that a user returns to the same instance
change the code to write reports to Amazon S3
a shared Amazon EFS file system
decision.choice: One Amazon EFS file system, mounted by the web tier and by the conversion workers.
decision.tradeoff: File storage costs more for each gigabyte than Amazon S3. Reports move to Amazon S3 when the code is rewritten.

question.text: A volume, a file system or a bucket for these files: how do I decide?

23.diagram: Before: three instances, each with its own volume; the download reaches the wrong instance. After: all instances mount one file system through a mount target in each Availability Zone.

adds: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
later.note: For Peldon's 12 TB of Windows file shares, joined to AWS Managed Microsoft AD (chapter 39).

23.note: The shared work directory holds the parts of long recordings that several workers convert. Not used: Amazon FSx for Lustre, FSx for NetApp ONTAP, FSx for OpenZFS.

24.title: AWS Backup and backup strategy
24.trigger: The bank asks for the backup policy of every data store, proof of last month's backups, and a restore test.
24.problem: Callvale's data is in Amazon Aurora, Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon EFS and Amazon EBS, in several accounts. Each service has different backup settings. The bank requires daily backups kept for 30 days and monthly backups kept for 7 years. Administrators must not be able to delete backups.
adds: backup vault with AWS Backup Vault Lock

options: the backup settings of each service, plus a written policy
custom programs that create snapshots on a schedule
AWS Backup plans for the whole organization
decision.choice: AWS Backup: one plan that selects resources by tag in every account, and a locked vault.
decision.tradeoff: A second policy layer sits above the services' own backups. Seven-year copies cost storage for data that is rarely restored.

question.text: If an attacker gets administrator access in production, can the attacker delete our backups?

24.diagram: Before: four data stores, four backup settings, no common report. After: one backup plan selects by tag, writes to a locked vault, and copies to a second account.

later.note: To US West (Oregon) (chapter 40).

24.note: Recordings in Amazon S3 are protected by S3 Versioning, S3 Object Lock and replication, not by AWS Backup.

25.title: Storage Gateway, DataSync, Snow Family and Transfer Family
25.trigger: The bank's storage holds 80 TB of old recordings and will be turned off in 30 days. Dorrin Health wants to send a nightly SFTP batch.
25.problem: The bank holds 80 TB of old recordings in its data center, in 6.7 million files. The files must be in Amazon S3 within 30 days. A VPN test reached 100 Mbps. The bank allows 500 Mbps on the Direct Connect connection.
adds: AWS Storage Gateway (Amazon S3 File Gateway)

options: custom copy programs through the VPN (74 days)
an AWS Snow Family device
AWS DataSync through Direct Connect (15 days)
decision.choice: AWS DataSync through Direct Connect at 500 Mbps: about 15 days.
decision.tradeoff: The import uses the bank's Direct Connect allowance for about 15 days, next to the nightly recordings.

question.text: 80 terabytes: do we send it through the network or do we ship storage devices?

25.diagram: Three paths into the audio bucket: the archive through DataSync and Direct Connect; the bank's recorder through an S3 File Gateway; Dorrin Health's nightly batch through an SFTP endpoint.
25.note: The archive lands under the prefix ostell/archive/ in S3 Standard-IA. The bank's recorder can only write to a file share, so an S3 File Gateway runs in the bank's data center. Dorrin Health sends 6,000 recordings (about 70 GB) at 01:00 to sftp.callvale.example. Snow Family: check the current device status in the canon before you state why it was not chosen.

26.title: Amazon RDS
26.trigger: PostgreSQL runs on one instance that Ben patches by hand. A second customer asks how fast Callvale recovers from a failure.
26.problem: Callvale runs PostgreSQL on one EC2 instance. Ben applies patches and checks backups by hand. If the instance or its Availability Zone fails, the application stops until Ben restores a snapshot. Callvale needs automatic failover and automatic backups without changes to the application.

options: a second database instance with replication that Ben builds
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with a Multi-AZ deployment
move the data to Amazon DynamoDB
decision.choice: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with a Multi-AZ deployment in the private data subnets.
decision.tradeoff: Callvale pays for a standby that serves no queries, and has less control of the operating system.

question.text: We pay for two databases but we use one. What do we get for the second one?

26.diagram: Before: one database instance with a data volume and daily snapshots. After: a primary and a standby in two Availability Zones behind one endpoint.

later.note: After 900 connections on launch day. The read replica serves dashboard queries.
Amazon Aurora replaces this database at month 20 (chapter 27).

26.note: The database instance of chapter 16 and its data volume are deleted after a final snapshot.

27.title: Amazon Aurora
27.trigger: With the bank, the database grows from 400 GB to 1.2 TB. At peak the read replica is 40 seconds behind, and dashboards show old data.
27.problem: Callvale's PostgreSQL database holds 1.2 TB, and 90% of queries are reads. At peak, the one read replica is up to 40 seconds behind the primary. Callvale needs several replicas behind one endpoint, fast failover, and a path to a second Region. The application must stay PostgreSQL-compatible.
adds: two Aurora Replicas and the reader endpoint
Aurora Serverless v2 for dev and staging

options: a larger RDS instance with more read replicas
Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL
a cache for all dashboard reads
decision.choice: An Aurora PostgreSQL cluster with one writer and two Aurora Replicas in three Availability Zones.
decision.tradeoff: A migration with a short cutover, and a new cost model to learn.

question.text: It is still PostgreSQL. What do I get from Aurora that RDS did not give me?

27.diagram: Before: an RDS primary, a standby and one slow read replica. After: an Aurora cluster with one writer and two replicas; the application uses the cluster endpoint and the reader endpoint.

later.note: A secondary cluster in US West (Oregon) (chapter 40).

27.note: Dev and staging are used for 50 hours a week. Their databases use Aurora Serverless v2.

28.title: Amazon DynamoDB
28.trigger: On launch day, each call's status row in PostgreSQL is updated 12 times. Row locks and 900 connections stop the database.
28.problem: Each call has one job record that the pipeline updates about 12 times. Writes are spiky, from 2 calls a minute at night to 40 at peak. The pipeline reads and writes by call ID and lists one customer's jobs by time. The pipeline needs no joins.

options: a larger PostgreSQL instance for the job rows
Amazon DynamoDB with on-demand capacity
Amazon ElastiCache for job state
decision.choice: A DynamoDB table, jobs, with on-demand capacity and one global secondary index.
decision.tradeoff: Access patterns must be known first. A new query can need a new index, and there are no SQL joins.

question.text: On-demand or provisioned capacity? I do not know my traffic yet.

28.diagram: Before: every pipeline step updates one PostgreSQL table through 900 connections. After: the steps write to the jobs table by call ID; the dashboard lists jobs through the index.

later.note: A replica table in US West (Oregon) (chapter 40). Provisioned capacity after the cost review (chapter 41).

28.note: Pipeline state P2 before, P3 after, shared with chapter 32. Job records are deleted 90 days after the call. Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is weighed at stage 4 for the live screen and is not used.

29.title: ElastiCache and caching
29.trigger: On launch day, users are signed out each time the Auto Scaling group removes an instance. Sessions live in instance memory.
29.problem: Callvale keeps user sessions in the memory of each web instance and uses sticky sessions. When an instance is removed, its users are signed out. The 20 most common dashboard queries cause 80% of database reads. Results can be up to 60 seconds old.
adds: Amazon ElastiCache replication group in two Availability Zones

options: keep sticky sessions and scale in slowly
sessions in Amazon DynamoDB and one more read replica
Amazon ElastiCache for sessions and for query results
decision.choice: Amazon ElastiCache holds the sessions and the results of the 20 queries for 60 seconds. Sticky sessions are turned off.
decision.tradeoff: A cached result can be 60 seconds old. The cache is one more cluster to size and to pay for.

question.text: On launch day, users were signed out in the middle of their work. Why, and can it happen again?

29.diagram: Before: sessions inside each instance; every dashboard request reaches the database. After: stateless instances; sessions and hot query results in the cache; only cache misses reach the database.
29.note: Engine: use the engine name that the canon gives as current for a new ElastiCache cluster.

30.title: Redshift and purpose-built databases
30.trigger: Ana's board reports join usage, billing and sales data from both companies. Peldon's product arrives with 200 GB in MongoDB.
30.problem: Callvale's finance team runs complex SQL joins on usage and billing data all day from a business intelligence tool. Separately, Peldon's application stores 200 GB in MongoDB, and its code cannot be rewritten this year. Callvale wants a managed service for each workload.

options: load everything into Amazon Aurora
MongoDB and a warehouse on EC2 instances
Amazon Redshift for reporting and Amazon DocumentDB for the MongoDB workload
decision.choice: Amazon Redshift for finance reporting. Amazon DocumentDB for Peldon's MongoDB data.
decision.tradeoff: Two more database engines to know and to pay for. MongoDB compatibility must be tested for the features that Peldon uses.

question.text: We already have Athena on the data lake. Why do you propose a data warehouse too?

30.diagram: A map of Callvale's data stores by data shape: Aurora, DynamoDB, ElastiCache, OpenSearch Service, Redshift, DocumentDB. Neptune and Keyspaces are greyed: not used.
30.note: Not used: Amazon Neptune, Amazon Keyspaces.

31.title: SQS, SNS and EventBridge
31.trigger: Launch day, 10:20 Eastern. The web tier scales out, but each upload request waits for the one worker. In 47 minutes, 1,900 uploads fail.
31.problem: After each upload, Callvale's web application calls the worker and waits. On launch day, the worker was overloaded and 1,900 uploads failed. No upload can be lost again, and one failed recording must not block the others. Several systems must learn when a transcript is ready.
adds: Amazon SQS queues (uploads, convert) with dead-letter queues
Amazon SNS topic transcript-ready with two subscribed queues (webhooks, indexing)

options: more and larger workers behind an internal load balancer
Amazon SQS queues, with an Amazon SNS topic for results
one stream for all events
decision.choice: SQS queues between the stages, an SNS topic that fans out results, and EventBridge for AWS events and schedules.
decision.tradeoff: Processing is asynchronous: users see 'processing', and workers must handle the same message twice without harm.

question.text: SQS, SNS, EventBridge: all three move messages. When do I use which?

31.diagram: Before: web tier, direct call, one overloaded worker. After: S3 event, uploads queue, pipeline, SNS topic transcript-ready, then the webhooks queue and the indexing queue; a dead-letter queue under each queue.
31.note: Pipeline state P1 before, P2 after, shared with chapter 18. A message moves to the dead-letter queue after 3 failed receives. EventBridge schedules replace the scheduled jobs for nightly work; EventBridge rules route AWS service events to the ops-alerts topic from stage 3.

32.title: Step Functions, Amazon MQ and AppFlow
32.trigger: The new pipeline is a chain of functions that call each other and wait in loops. Nobody can see where a call stopped.
32.problem: Callvale processes each call in six steps: convert, transcribe, analyze, summarize, save, notify. Functions call each other and wait in loops, with retries written by hand. AWS Step Functions

Amazon API Gateway in front of the web tier

adds: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams stream live-events

options: one Amazon SQS queue for each consumer
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with Amazon Data Firehose
Amazon MSK
decision.choice: A Kinesis data stream, live-events, with the call ID as partition key. Data Firehose delivers every event to the data lake.

load all data into a data warehouse cluster
a data lake in Amazon S3 with AWS Glue and Amazon Athena

open-source models on GPU instances that Callvale manages

Prometheus and Grafana that Callvale runs on EC2
Amazon CloudWatch, AWS CloudTrail and AWS X-Ray

custom programs that call the AWS CLI

move the VMware environment to VMware Cloud on AWS
rehost the servers and convert the database

40.title: High availability and disaster recovery
40.trigger: The bank contract sets an RPO of 15 minutes and an RTO of 1 hour for the loss of a Region. The first test is due at month 27.
40.problem: Callvale runs in one Region, across three Availability Zones. A bank contract requires an RPO of 15 minutes and an RTO of 1 hour if the whole Region fails. A test must prove it every 6 months. Ana wants the lowest cost that meets these numbers.

options: backup and restore
pilot light
warm standby
multi-site active/active
decision.choice: Warm standby in US West (Oregon): data replicates all the time, and one task of each service is always running.
decision.tradeoff: Callvale pays all month for a small second copy of every service.

question.text: If the Virginia Region fails, what do I tell the bank, and what does the standby cost me in a normal month?

41.title: Cost optimization

S3 Lifecycle rule to S3 Glacier Deep Archive

options: Reserved Instances for everything that runs today
a Compute Savings Plan, Spot Instances, storage lifecycle rules and schedules
move all workloads to a cheaper Region
decision.choice: A Compute Savings Plan for 70% of the steady compute. Spot Instances for the workers. S3 Glacier Deep Archive for 87 TB. Dev and staging stop outside working hours.
decision.tradeoff: The commitment is paid even if usage falls. Archived recordings take hours to restore; customers accept up to 48 hours.

question.text: Where does the money go, and what can we cut this quarter with no effect on customers?

follow one recording through four layers

question.text: For this one recording, show me every place where access could be allowed by mistake.

43.title: Decoupling, scaling and caching patterns
43.trigger: Ben writes the review of launch day. He lists five places where one slow part stopped another part.
43.problem: On launch day, Callvale's web tier scaled out and the system still failed. Uploads waited for one worker, and every step updated one database table. Sessions and report files lived on single instances. Callvale must remove each coupling with little change to the code.
43.adds_note: Nothing new. The chapter reviews the launch-week changes of chapters 15, 17, 18, 23, 26, 28, 29, 31, 32 and 33.

options: larger instances in every tier
rewrite the product in small services now
fix the five couplings one by one
decision.choice: Fix each coupling with one managed part. The parts are a queue, a scaling policy, a job table, a cache with a shared file system, and a topic.
decision.tradeoff: The system has more parts and is asynchronous, so the team needs tracing and must expect duplicate and late messages.

question.text: We scaled the web tier and the system still failed. What did we miss?

43.diagram: The launch-day path drawn twice. Before: a chain in which each part waits for the next. After: the same path with a queue, a scaling policy, a job table, a cache and a topic at the five numbered couplings.
43.note: The five couplings, in fixed order: 1 the upload request waits for the worker; 2 one worker cannot grow with the backlog; 3 every step updates one PostgreSQL table; 4 sessions and report files live on single instances; 5 the pipeline calls the webhook sender and the search indexer one after the other.
